title: How to Perform a Ping Check with Grafana Cloud Synthetic Monitoring

blocks.content:
A ping check is the simplest synthetic check there is. It sends ICMP echo packets to a host from probes around the world and records whether the host answered and how long it took.

That makes it the right tool for three jobs: confirming a host is reachable at all, tracking round-trip latency from real geographic locations, and catching an outage before your users report it. What it does not do is test your application, so pair it with an HTTP check when you care about what the endpoint returns.

In this guide you'll create a ping check against a host, choose where it runs from, and turn on an alert for when it stops answering.

blocks.title: How To Ping Check with Grafana Cloud Synthetic Monitoring

blocks.content: Every check type lives behind the **API Endpoint** form, so that is where you start. To open it, complete the following step:
Open **Create new check** and choose **API Endpoint**. Ping, HTTP, DNS, TCP, and Traceroute checks are all configured from this one form.
The editor opens on **Request**, the first of five numbered steps down the left-hand side.
A check needs three things before it can run: a name, a protocol, and something to talk to. To supply them, complete the following steps:

In **Job name**, enter a name for the check. It becomes the `job` label on every metric the check writes, so pick something you will recognise on a dashboard.

**MyApp:Ping** is filled in for you.
blocks.tooltip: Grouping related checks under one job name makes them easy to query together later.

blocks.content: Set **Request type** to **Ping**. This switches the form to ICMP and drops the HTTP-only fields such as method and headers.
blocks.tooltip: Ping tests reachability at the network layer, so it answers even when the web server behind it is down.

blocks.content:
In **Request target**, enter the hostname or IP address to ping.

**grafana.com** is filled in for you.
blocks.tooltip: A ping target is a host, not a URL, so leave off the scheme and any path.

blocks.content: That is a working check. Everything from here on is tuning.

blocks.alt: Synthetic Monitoring application in Grafana Cloud, showing the API Endpoint check creation page with Ping selected as the request type

blocks.content: Steps 2 and 3 cover how long to wait for a reply and how to label the results. To review them, complete the following steps:
Open **Uptime**.
**Timeout** is how long a probe waits for a reply before recording the attempt as failed. The default suits most hosts, but raise it if you are pinging somewhere genuinely distant from your probes.
blocks.tooltip: A timeout shorter than your real round-trip time will report an outage that is not happening.

blocks.content: Open **Labels**.
Add a label. Labels are attached to the check's metrics, so they are how you filter a dashboard down to one service or one environment later.

steps.tooltip: The label name is the dimension you will group or filter by.
Keep values to a small, predictable set so the metric stays cheap to query.

blocks.content: Labels cost nothing now and save you a lot of filtering once you have more than a handful of checks.
Where a check runs from decides what it can tell you. To choose probes and frequency, complete the following steps:
Open **Execution**.
Select at least one probe. **North California** is highlighted as a starting point, and picking a few spread across regions is what turns a reachability check into a latency comparison.
blocks.tooltip: One probe tells you whether a host is up. Several tell you whether a problem is global or regional.

blocks.content: **Frequency** is how often every probe runs the check. One minute is the default and a sensible starting point.
blocks.tooltip: Each probe runs on its own schedule, so more probes at a higher frequency means proportionally more executions.

blocks.content: Your check now runs from real locations on a fixed schedule.

blocks.alt: Synthetic Monitoring application in Grafana Cloud, showing the API Endpoint check creation page in the Execution step, with North California, Singapore, and Frankfurt selected

blocks.content: A check nobody looks at is not monitoring. To alert on it and save, complete the following steps:
Open **Alerting**.
Enable **Probe Failed Executions**. This is the outage alert: it fires when enough probes stop getting a reply.
blocks.tooltip: Requiring more than one failed execution avoids paging someone over a single dropped packet.

blocks.content: **Ping Request Duration** is the slow-but-up alert. Reachability alerts stay quiet while latency climbs, so this is the one that catches a host degrading rather than failing.
blocks.tooltip: Worth enabling once you know your normal round-trip time, so the threshold means something.

blocks.content: Click **Test** to run the check once, right now, without saving it. This is the quickest way to catch a typo in the target.
blocks.tooltip: A test run uses your selected probes but does not create the check or write metrics.

blocks.content: Click **Save**. The check starts running immediately and its first results appear within a couple of minutes.
Your ping check is live, running from the probes you chose, and will alert you when the host stops answering.

From here, the check's own dashboard shows uptime, reachability, and latency broken down by probe, which is where a regional problem becomes obvious. Adding an HTTP check against the same host is the usual next step, since ping tells you the host is up and HTTP tells you your application is.
